'''''Lepidium campestre''''', the '''field pepperwort''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref>  '''field peppercress, field peppergrass, field pepperweed''' or '''field cress''', is usually a [[biennial plant|biennial]] with some form of [[annual plant]] in the [[Brassicaceae]] or [[Mustard plant|mustard]] family, native to [[Europe]], but commonly found in [[North America]] as an [[invasive species|invasive]] [[noxious weed|weed]]. The most notable characteristic of field pepperweed is the [[raceme]] of flowers which forks off of the stem.  These racemes are made up of first small white flowers and later green, flat and oval seedpods each about 6 mm long and 4 mm wide.<ref name=uva>Richard H. Uva, Joseph C. Neal and Joseph M. Ditomaso, ''Weeds of The Northeast'', (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1997), Pp. 176-177.</ref> Each seedpod contains two brown, 2.5 mm long seeds.

The stem of field pepperweed comes out of a [[basal rosette]] of toothed leaves. The stem is covered in leaves, which are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], alternate and arrow-shaped.<ref name=uva/> The entire plant is generally between 20 and 60 cm tall and covered in small hairs.<ref name=uva/>

==Cultivation and uses==
Field pepperweed grows in disturbed land, crops, and waste places.<ref name=uva/> It can tolerate most soils.

The plant is edible. The young leaves can be eaten as greens, added raw to [[salad]]s or boiled for ten minutes.<ref name=peterson>Lee Allen Peterson, ''Edible Wild Plants,'' (New York City: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1977), p. 26.</ref>  The young fruits and seeds can be used as a spice, with a taste between [[black pepper]] and mustard. The leaves contain [[protein]], [[vitamin A]] and [[vitamin C]].<ref name=peterson/>

==Domestication==
Field cress has been targeted for domestication at the [[Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences]] (SLU), because it holds high agronomic promise as a biennial/perennial oilseed crop as it has many good characteristics of a high-yielding winter-hardy crop.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/2107/|title = Towards the domestication of Lepidium campestre as an undersown oilseed crop| journal=Acta Universitatis Agriculturae Sueciae |year = 2009| issue=65 | last1=Eriksson | first1=Dennis | volume=2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Merker|first1=Arnuf|last2=Nilsson|first2=Peter|title=Some oil crop properties in wild Barbarea and Lepidium species|journal=Swedish Journal of Agricultural Research|date=1995|doi=10.1080/09064719809362493|volume=48|pages=159–164|doi-access=free}}</ref> Unlike any other oilseed crop, field cress can be highly productive in the northern parts of temperate regions and has been successfully grown in Umeå, Sweden (40 km south of the Arctic Circle) where it can yield correspondingly 3.3 tons/ha. In addition, field cress provides important [[ecosystem services]] as it functions as a cover crop during winter and can be undersown a spring cereal.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/09064710902903747 | volume=60 | title=Barley yield increases with undersownLepidium campestre | year=2010 | journal=Acta Agriculturae Scandinavica, Section B | pages=269–273 | last1 = Merker | first1 = Arnulf | last2 = Eriksson | first2 = Dennis | last3 = Bertholdsson | first3 = Nils-Ove| issue=3 | s2cid=84293246 | doi-access=free }}</ref> The oil of field cress is suitable for different industrial applications such as production of [[hydrotreated vegetable oil]] diesel (HVO). The researchers at SLU have identified and mapped several genes in field cress that are known to be important for domestication related traits such as flowering time, pod shattering and seed dormancy.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1186/s12863-018-0624-9 | volume=19 | title=Identification of genes regulating traits targeted for domestication of field cress (Lepidium campestre) as a biennial and perennial oilseed crop | year=2018 | journal=BMC Genetics | last1 = Gustafsson | first1 = Cecilia | last2 = Willforss | first2 = Jakob | last3 = Lopes-Pinto | first3 = Fernando | last4 = Ortiz | first4 = Rodomiro | last5 = Geleta | first5 = Mulatu| issue=1 | page=36 | pmid=29843613 | pmc = 5975587 | doi-access=free }}</ref>
